articles.title: British wedding venue shut down after workers found five World War II bombs while digging for solar panels; guests and residents forced to leave while explosives were detonated
articles.summary: What began as an ordinary construction project to make a wedding venue more sustainable turned into a wartime mystery when workers digging into the ground
articles.body: What began as an ordinary construction project to make a wedding venue more sustainable turned into a wartime mystery when workers digging into the ground uncovered five suspected World War II bombs buried beneath the property. The mud-covered objects initially looked like broken water or gas pipes, but a closer inspection revealed metal fins that raised alarm. Within hours, a wedding venue in England's picturesque Cotswolds region was shut down, a safety cordon was established and nearby residents, businesses and people at the site were evacuated while bomb disposal specialists examined the potentially dangerous discovery.The incident occurred on November 2, 2026, at The Great Tythe Barn and Thythe House in Long Newnton, near Tetbury, Gloucestershire. According to the BBC and PEOPLE, construction workers discovered the suspected explosives while digging a trench for a planned solar field. Gloucestershire Police were alerted that morning, prompting an emergency response and the establishment of a 200-metre exclusion zone around the site. The discovery brought work at the venue to an abrupt halt, with authorities asking people to stay away while specialists assessed the objects and determined how to dispose of them safely.Workers initially mistook bombs for old pipesThe two workers who discovered the objects were head gardener Kevin Roberts and subcontractor John Blundell. They were digging a trench for the planned solar field when they came across the suspected explosives. Speaking to the Wilts and Gloucestershire Standard, Roberts said the discovery happened within minutes of starting the excavation. The pair uncovered five objects that they believed could be live mortars.Blundell recalled that the objects initially appeared to be broken sections of a gas main or an old water pipe. After picking them up and clearing away the mud, however, the workers noticed features that made them suspect the objects were World War II mortars. The metal flight fins proved particularly significant. Once they recognised what the objects might be, the workers put them down, moved away and contacted the police.Their discovery illustrates the risks posed by unexploded wartime ordnance that can remain buried for decades. Even when such objects appear corroded or resemble ordinary construction debris, their condition cannot be judged safely by appearance alone.Wedding venue and surrounding area evacuatedGloucestershire Police responded after receiving a report of suspected unexploded ordnance near Tetbury on the morning of November 2. Officers established a 200-metre cordon to protect the public while specialist personnel attended.Nearby residents and businesses were evacuated as a precaution, and the wedding venue closed its entire site. PEOPLE reported that workers and guests who had remained at the property following a weekend wedding were also evacuated.The venue announced on social media that it was closed following the discovery of historical artefacts. In a statement shared with the Wilts and Gloucestershire Standard, it confirmed that five items believed to be World War II bombs had been found on its grounds.The venue said it had contacted the police immediately and that the area had been cordoned off while bomb disposal specialists were called in to assess the objects. It also warned that further items had been found and that the evacuation zone might need to be extended. A separate local report by Wiltshire 999s likewise said additional suspected explosives had been discovered.The emergency response meant that the planned solar installation had to take a back seat while authorities focused on ensuring the safety of people in the surrounding area.German bombs destroyed in controlled detonationAn Explosive Ordnance Disposal operator examined the objects and identified the bombs as German, according to an Army spokesperson quoted by the Wilts and Gloucestershire Standard. Police later confirmed that the devices were destroyed in a controlled detonation. The operation took place after specialists assessed the suspected explosives and determined how they could be dealt with safely.A controlled detonation is a specialist disposal procedure intended to manage the risks associated with explosive devices. It is carried out by trained personnel under controlled conditions rather than by attempting to handle or dismantle the objects without expert assessment.The discovery also served as a reminder that the consequences of World War II remain visible in parts of Britain long after the conflict ended. Construction and excavation projects can occasionally uncover wartime objects that have remained underground for generations. articles.title: EUA: Talarico é 1º democrata eleito senador pelo Texas em 38 anos | G1
articles.standfirst: James Talarico, deputado estadual democrata desde 2018 e ex-professor da rede pública, enfrentou o republicano Ken Paxton, procurador-geral do estado desde 2015.
articles.summary: James Talarico, deputado estadual democrata desde 2018 e ex-professor da rede pública, enfrentou o republicano Ken Paxton, procurador-geral do estado desde 2015.
articles.body:
James Talarico e Ken Paxton disputam vaga no Texas — Foto: Kaylee Greenlee/Reuters; Evan Vucci/Pool photo via AP

O democrata James Talarico venceu a eleição para o Senado pelo Texas.

O estado é tradicionalmente conservador - o último democrata a levar a cadeira do Senado foi Lloyd Bentsen, em 1988 .

James Talarico, deputado estadual democrata desde 2018 e ex-professor da rede pública, enfrentou o republicano Ken Paxton, procurador-geral do estado desde 2015.

Talarico ganhou projeção no Texas com vídeos virais nas redes sociais em que critica a aproximação entre religião e políticas conservadoras. Também adotou um discurso populista contra grandes empresas, bilionários e a influência do dinheiro na política.

Paxton, por sua vez, é um dos principais nomes da direita trumpista no estado e teve o apoio de Donald Trump. Em um estado de fronteira, defendeu políticas migratórias mais rígidas, restrições ao aborto e ampliação do acesso a armas.

Sua trajetória, porém, é marcada por controvérsias: em 2023, sofreu um processo de impeachment na Câmara estadual por acusações de corrupção e abuso de poder, mas foi absolvido. Também respondeu a um processo por fraude de valores mobiliários, encerrado por meio de um acordo.

Campanha teve teorias da conspiração e dinheiro de Musk

O candidato democrata foi alvo de teorias da conspiração, quando, no fim de setembro, ficou nove dias afastado da campanha por uma gripe. Foi o suficiente para que seus opositores espalhassem o boato de que ele estaria internado em uma clínica psiquiátrica e que o presidente Donald Trump afirmasse, sem provas, que Talarico é vegano e teria comido carne para obter ganhos políticos.

Ao mesmo tempo, Elon Musk gastou mais de 150 milhões de dólares do próprio bolso para apoiar Paxton. Para fazer frente ao rival, o candidato democrata focou a campanha na união e na fé.

O candidato democrata ao Senado pelo Texas, nos Estados Unidos, James Talarico, durante campanha na cidade de Dallas, em 29 de outubro de 2026. — Foto: Mike Segar/ Reuters

articles.standfirst: Seleção exige nível superior e oferece oportunidades em quatro áreas, incluindo auditoria e tecnologia da informação. Prazo termina às 18h, e a taxa de inscrição é de R$ 170.
articles.summary: Seleção exige nível superior e oferece oportunidades em quatro áreas, incluindo auditoria e tecnologia da informação. Prazo termina às 18h, e a taxa de inscrição é de R$ 170.
articles.body:
Fachada da Controladoria-Geral da União (CGU) — Foto: Kenzo Suzuki ASCOM/CGU

As inscrições para o novo concurso público da Controladoria-Geral da União ( CGU ) terminam nesta quarta-feira (4), às 18h (horário de Brasília) . Ao todo, são oferecidas 60 vagas imediatas, além de cadastro de reserva .

A taxa de inscrição é de R$ 170 e pode ser paga até 6 de novembro. Podem solicitar a isenção da taxa os candidatos inscritos no Cadastro Único para Programas Sociais do Governo Federal (CadÚnico) e os doadores de medula óssea cadastrados em entidades reconhecidas pelo Ministério da Saúde.

As oportunidades são destinadas a candidatos com nível superior. O salário inicial é de R$ 20 mil para uma jornada de 40 horas semanais .

As 60 vagas estão distribuídas da seguinte forma:

Tecnologia da Informação (TI) – Ciência de Dados: 10 vagas;

TI – Desenvolvimento de Sistemas: 10 vagas.

Para o cargo de Auditoria, são oferecidas 20 vagas na sede da CGU, em Brasília, e outras 10 distribuídas entre as unidades regionais do Acre, Amapá, Mato Grosso, Rondônia e Roraima, com duas vagas em cada estado.

As três áreas de Tecnologia da Informação (TI) têm lotação no Distrito Federal e oferecem 10 vagas imediatas cada.

O concurso prevê a possibilidade de aprovação de até 368 candidatos no total , incluindo os classificados dentro do número de vagas imediatas.

Desse limite, até 206 aprovados serão para o cargo de Auditoria e até 54 para cada uma das três especialidades de Tecnologia da Informação (TI). Os demais aprovados poderão compor o cadastro de reserva.

O concurso reserva 5% das vagas para pessoas com deficiência (PcD). Além disso, 30% das oportunidades são destinadas a ações afirmativas: 25% para pessoas pretas e pardas, 3% para indígenas e 2% para quilombolas.

As provas objetiva e discursiva serão aplicadas em 13 de dezembro , em todas as capitais do país ( veja o cronograma completo abaixo ).

A avaliação será dividida em dois turnos . Pela manhã, os candidatos responderão à prova objetiva, com duração de cinco horas. À tarde, será aplicada a etapa discursiva, com duração de três horas e meia.

A prova objetiva terá 170 itens no modelo de julgamento “certo ou errado” , distribuídos em três blocos: 40 de conhecimentos básicos, 40 de conhecimentos complementares e 90 de conhecimentos específicos.

Já a prova discursiva será composta por duas questões. A primeira abordará conhecimentos complementares e valerá 30 pontos. A segunda trará uma situação-problema relacionada à área específica do cargo e valerá 70 pontos.

Os locais e horários individuais de aplicação das provas serão divulgados em 2 de dezembro . Os candidatos deverão comparecer ao local designado com pelo menos uma hora de antecedência em relação ao início da avaliação.

O concurso terá validade de dois anos a partir da homologação do resultado final no Diário Oficial da União (DOU), podendo ser prorrogado uma única vez por igual período.

Prazo final para pagamento da taxa de inscrição: 6 de novembro de 2026

Consulta aos locais de prova: 2 de dezembro de 2026

Aplicação das provas objetiva e discursiva: 13 de dezembro de 2026

Resultado definitivo das provas objetivas: 14 de janeiro de 2027

Resultado final da prova discursiva e resultado final do concurso: 15 de abril de 2027

articles.title: RS registra 67 feminicídios em 2026; saiba como pedir ajuda | G1
articles.standfirst: Dois crimes registrados nos últimos dias elevaram o número de vítimas no estado. Canais de denúncia e iniciativas de conscientização buscam ampliar a proteção às mulheres.
articles.summary: Dois crimes registrados nos últimos dias elevaram o número de vítimas no estado. Canais de denúncia e iniciativas de conscientização buscam ampliar a proteção às mulheres.
articles.body:
O Rio Grande do Sul chegou a 67 vítimas de feminicídio em 2026 . Os dois casos mais recentes foram registrados nesta semana, entre domingo (1º) e segunda-feira (2), e reforçaram a gravidade da violência contra as mulheres no estado.

O crime mais recente aconteceu na localidade de Rincão das Boeiras, no interior de Itacurubi , na Região Central. A vítima foi Antônia Bueno Flores , 64 anos. Segundo a polícia, ela foi morta pelo companheiro, Luiz Alvarenga Rodrigues, 66 anos. Conforme a investigação, não havia medida protetiva em vigor.

Já em Sobradinho , Júlia Roseli da Silva , 45 anos, foi morta na noite de domingo dentro da casa do ex-companheiro. De acordo com informações repassadas por familiares, o homem não aceitava o término do relacionamento.

Júlia havia registrado ocorrência contra ele e chegou a obter duas medidas protetivas , em 2021 e 2023, mas não contava mais com a proteção. Ela deixou dois filhos.

Sinal de ajuda de violência contra a mulher — Foto: Reprodução/ RBS TV

Conhecido internacionalmente como sinal de ajuda , o gesto de alerta de que uma mulher está em perigo surgiu no Canadá durante a pandemia de Covid-19 . A ideia era permitir que vítimas que conviviam com seus agressores conseguissem pedir socorro de forma discreta, sem despertar suspeitas.

Segundo Nadia Bisch, fundadora e diretora do Instituto Lótus, é importante que cada vez mais pessoas conheçam o significado do sinal .

"Quanto mais a gente trouxer de informação de que isso sinaliza situação de violência, que isso pode ser um pedido de socorro, mais chances temos de que alguém consiga ajudar", afirma.

Ela explica que, ao identificar o gesto, uma pessoa pode anotar os dados da vítima, acionar a polícia e encaminhar o caso para atendimento.

Banco Vermelho de enfrentamento à violência contra a mulher — Foto: Reprodução/ RBS TV

Outro símbolo utilizado no combate à violência de gênero está presente em ruas e praças: os bancos vermelhos .

A iniciativa, que começou na Itália em 2016 , busca chamar a atenção para os feminicídios e orientar a população sobre onde buscar ajuda. Os bancos exibem informações sobre canais de denúncia e atendimento às vítimas .

Coordenadora nacional do projeto Bancos Vermelhos Oficial no Brasil, Denise Argemi afirma que a cor faz referência ao sangue das mulheres assassinadas em crimes de gênero.

"Nós temos um slogan, é o sangue derramado por homens que diziam amar essas mulheres. Esse é o mesmo slogan da Itália e é o que nós utilizamos aqui", explica Denise.

Em Porto Alegre , os bancos já foram instalados em 10 praças da Capital , além de órgãos públicos e locais de grande circulação, por meio de parceria com a prefeitura.

A proposta é levar o debate para espaços frequentados diariamente pela população e ampliar a conscientização sobre a necessidade de enfrentar a violência contra as mulheres.

O telefone 190 , da Brigada Militar, deve ser acionado em situações de emergência ou quando a violência estiver acontecendo naquele momento .

Já o número 180 , canal do Ministério das Mulheres, recebe denúncias, orienta vítimas e fornece informações sobre direitos e formas de atendimento .

O Rio Grande do Sul ocupa a quinta posição entre os estados com maior número de denúncias registradas no 180 . Em 2026, já foram contabilizados mais de 5,3 mil relatos de violência doméstica . A maioria das comunicações foi feita pelas próprias vítimas.

As denúncias recebidas pelo canal são encaminhadas pelo governo federal à Polícia Civil, responsável pela investigação dos casos.

Segundo o delegado Juliano Ferreira, qualquer pessoa pode colaborar com informações.

"Toda informação repassada é anônima. O importante é que ela chegue às autoridades com o máximo de detalhes possível para que possamos identificar o fato, a vítima ou o agressor", afirma.

No estado, também é possível realizar pedidos de medida protetiva online e denúncias pelo WhatsApp 55 (51) 984440606.

articles.title: Contaminação em São Tomé de Paripe têm 9 meses de praia interditada | G1
articles.standfirst: Pescadores, marisqueiras e barraqueiros protestaram na terça-feira (3), por falta de respostas dos órgãos público. Praia no Subúrbio de Salvador segue interditada, mas sem placas e barreiras.
articles.summary: Pescadores, marisqueiras e barraqueiros protestaram na terça-feira (3), por falta de respostas dos órgãos público. Praia no Subúrbio de Salvador segue interditada, mas sem placas e
articles.body:
A contaminação da praia de São Tomé de Paripe, no Subúrbio de Salvador , por Nitrato e Cobre, completa nove meses neste mês, sem solução.

Conforme apurou a TV Bahia, a praia segue interditada para banho, porém sem placas de aviso e nem barreiras. Trabalhadores que costumavam atuar na região também continuam afastados dos seus postos .

O caso envolve as empresas Gerdau e Intermarítima, após um vazamento de substâncias durante uma operação de transporte de materiais no terminal marítimo da região. Análises do Instituto do Meio Ambiente e Recursos Hídricos (Inema) identificaram a presença de substâncias contaminantes.

O instituto constatou que a contaminação partiu do Terminal Itapuã, que faz operações de estocagem e movimentação de granéis sólidos. Antes da interrupção, o terminal era operado pela empresa Intermarítima, mas por 30 anos a Gerdau administrou a operação. O Inema atribuiu a responsabilidade às duas companhias

No mês de junho, o Governo Federal reconheceu a situação de emergência em Salvador em decorrência da contaminação química registrada . A decisão foi publicada no Diário Oficial da União (DOU) pelo Ministério da Integração e do Desenvolvimento Regional, por meio de portaria assinada pelo secretário nacional de Proteção e Defesa Civil.

Em agosto, a Prefeitura de Salvador prorrogou por mais 90 dias a situação de emergência na região . A decisão considerou a permanência dos impactos sociais e ambientais provocados pelas substâncias químicas.

A situação também levou a Justiça Federal a determinar o bloqueio de aproximadamente R$ 387,6 milhões em bens das empresas investigadas. Em junho, o Inema já havia aplicado multas de R$ 20 milhões à Intermarítima e de R$ 50 milhões à Gerdau . Segundo o órgão, as duas empresas contribuíram para o cenário de contaminação. A Intermarítima, no entanto, afirma que não movimenta cargas relacionadas às substâncias encontradas na praia.

Nesta quinta-feira (3), moradores, pescadores e marisqueiros realizaram uma manifestação na altura da Base Naval, em São Tomé de Paripe. O grupo bloqueou a passagem de ônibus e outros veículos para cobrar o pagamento de indenizações prometidas às pessoas afetadas pela contaminação.

Em setembro, representantes de órgãos estaduais e federais, incluindo os Ministérios Públicos da Bahia (MP-BA) e Federal (MPF), se reuniram com a Gerdau para discutir medidas de reparação. Na ocasião, foi acordada a construção de um Termo de Ajustamento de Conduta (TAC), com previsão de pagamento de auxílio financeiro aos moradores afetados.

Segundo os manifestantes, até o momento, nenhum valor foi depositado.

O Ministério Público da Bahia (MP-BA) também tenta viabilizar um auxílio financeiro emergencial para as famílias que perderam sua fonte de renda. Em uma reunião anterior, as empresas recusaram a proposta de pagamento mensal de um salário mínimo às famílias afetadas.

A disputa sobre a responsabilidade pelos danos também dificulta o avanço das medidas de reparação. A Gerdau e a Intermarítima divergem sobre quem deve responder pela contaminação, enquanto pescadores e marisqueiros seguem sem poder trabalhar na área.

Em nota, a Gerdau informou que mantém diálogo com autoridades e órgãos competentes para construir uma solução social e técnico ambiental para a região. A empresa afirmou ainda que pretende contribuir com medidas de apoio à população e com o restabelecimento da normalidade. A equipe do g1 tentou contato com a empresa Intermarítima, mas não obteve resposta até a última atualização desta reportagem.

O Inema, também em nota, ressaltou que segue monitorando a área e fiscalizando o cumprimento das medidas em ambientais exigidas das empresas. Já a Prefeitura de Salvador, declarou que vem adotando medidas emergenciais de proteção social as famílias de alimentação e encaminhamento as redes de proteção.

Confira a cronologia da contaminação abaixo:

Fevereiro: Inicio da contaminação química por produtos associados a atividades de estocagem e movimentação de granéis sólidos no Terminal Itapuã.

Abril: No dia três de abril, ocorre denúncia sobre pesca com bomba e, em seis de abril, registra-se uma grande mortandade com cerca de 2 mil pescados recolhidos. Em 22 de abril, o tema domina debates na Câmara Municipal de Salvador.

Junho: Em 22 de junho, o Governo Federal reconhece a situação de emergência ambiental na região. O Inema aponta altos índices de cobre, compostos nitrogenados, nitrato, nitrito e nitrogênio amoniacal na água e sedimentos.

Julho: Em 27 de julho, o Ministério Público Federal (MPF) instaure inquérito civil sob condução do procurador Marcos André Carneiro Silva para investigar os impactos sobre comunidades pesqueiras e quilombolas.

Agosto: Em 20 de agosto, a Justiça Federal da Bahia determina o bloqueio de aproximadamente R$ 387,6 milhões em bens das empresas investigadas. A Prefeitura de Salvador prorroga a situação de emergência por mais 90 dias.

Setembro: Em 2 de setembro, moradores e marisqueiros propõem um auxílio emergencial em parcela única de R$ 12 mil para cerca de 2 mil famílias (rejeitando a contraproposta da Gerdau de R$ 1 mil por mês durante um ano). Em setembro, há discussões entre órgãos públicos e a Gerdau sobre acordos de pagamento que não são concretizados.

Novembro: Moradores, marisqueiras, pescadores e barraqueiras bloqueiam ruas e protestam contra a ausência de indenizações efetivas e a falta de descontaminação completa da praia.

articles.title: 'Multi-cancer' blood tests coming to some GP surgeries
articles.summary: The aim is to detect hard-to-diagnose abdominal cancers, including liver, ovarian and pancreatic cancer, much sooner.
articles.body:
New blood tests designed to check for multiple cancers in one go will be offered to NHS patients in some 200 GP surgeries in England as part of a trial.

The aim is to detect hard-to-diagnose abdominal cancers, including liver, ovarian and pancreatic cancer, much sooner. These cancers are often found only after they have spread.

The tests look for proteins or fragments of DNA in the blood that may signal cancer. Results could help doctors decide which patients with vague symptoms need further investigations.

More than 20,000 patients aged 45 and over with symptoms such as pain or persistent bloating will be eligible to take part.

The government-funded trial, led by the University of Birmingham, will assess whether the tests are accurate enough for wider NHS use.

The idea of a blood test that can identify multiple cancers is not new.

A separate NHS trial of a test called Galleri recently failed to meet its main goal of reducing diagnoses of late-stage cancers, although researchers are still assessing its potential benefits.

Prof Peter Johnson, NHS England's national clinical director for cancer, said detecting abdomen cancer early was "notoriously difficult" because symptoms can easily be mistaken for other less serious conditions.

Earlier diagnosis gives patients a much better chance of successful treatment and survival.

Around 71,000 people in England are diagnosed each year with pancreatic, stomach, liver, ovarian or bowel cancer, and nearly 35,000 die from these diseases.

The new STRIDE-RCT trial is about detecting bowel, small bowel, stomach, oesophageal, pancreatic, liver, bile duct and gallbladder, ovarian, endometrial, kidney, bladder and prostate cancer.

Patients will provide one or two tubes of blood, taken at their GP practice, alongside routine tests.

Scientists will then analyse the samples for signs of cancer and, if present, may be able to pinpoint where in the body the tumour is located.

A positive result does not automatically mean there is cancer, and a negative result is not a guaranteed all-clear.

Health secretary Yvette Cooper said she hoped simple blood tests such as these would help identify patients needing urgent investigation much sooner.

Michelle Mitchell from Cancer Research UK said: "GPs have long needed better tools to help them navigate that uncertainty by identifying which patients require further testing and this trial in England is an important step towards addressing that need."

articles.title: Graduates jobs: More work with AI but what else?
articles.summary: Graduates are spending more time managing AI, but are they missing out on other work experience?
articles.body:
Recent university graduate Lotte Underwood is a public relations executive with a twist - she spends more time using AI than actually doing PR.

Underwood, 25, joined London-based PR agency Fight or Flight in November last year, in the new role of "AI associate" after completing a degree and then a masters in marketing.

She's part of a recently established, dedicated AI team that has built around 30 AI agents. Specific tasks include industry research, client reporting, media interview preparation, helping clients create clearer briefs, and image generation.

A big part of Underwood's job is to manage those agents, check their outputs and feed those to the team members who are dealing directly with clients and the media.

Another key responsibility of hers is to monitor how clients appear in the responses from AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and others.

"A huge part is being in client meetings and calls to work out what is actually going to be most helpful from these agents," says Underwood.

AI is seen as one of the main factors behind graduate job cuts , but companies are also creating dedicated AI-specific graduate roles like Underwood's.

Dillan Patel, for example, joined engineering software company Stride 18 months ago as an intern. A business management graduate, he was put to work developing an internal chatbot designed to capture the knowledge of a senior staff member transitioning into retirement.

Patel, 24, is now an AI automation analyst, tasked with developing further internal agents to provide specific information to individual teams, while also identifying which manual or repetitive tasks across the company could be done by AI.

"My role focuses on finding practical ways to use technology, automation, data and AI to improve how we operate," says Coventry-based Patel.

Such AI savvy graduates are also in demand from companies like ArvatoConnect, an outsourced contact centre company.

CEO Debra Maxwell says the company's usual graduate intake is on hold this year, but she plans to resume it next year with a bigger focus on AI.

"We would be looking for more AI-disruptor type roles, where you can challenge us as an organisation to think more holistically about where AI can be applied and where we could grow our business from," says London-based Maxwell.

"We see our graduates as not filling administrative roles, but actually adding value to the organisation in a different way."

Maxwell adds: "For example, one of our recent graduates is using AI to do deep dives on specific markets, and provide more information for when we're bidding [for new contracts]. It's basically giving him a more rounded role."

If AI can make a graduate job bigger and more integral to the organisation, Maxwell argues that companies can create a more loyal, engaged workforce that is able to contribute more meaningfully, much earlier.

Research from consultancy PwC found that some graduate roles are assuming more responsibilities because of AI, as it allows companies to demand more senior abilities from junior hires.

For the consultancy's 2026 AI Jobs Barometer , it analysed 2.4 million entry-level jobs in the US. It found that the entry-level roles most influenced by AI are now seven times more likely to require traditionally senior-level skills. These include motivational leadership, strategic decision making and team building.

Those entry-level roles with higher expectations have in fact grown 35% since 2019, PwC found, while other entry-level roles actually shrank by 10%.

Cian Clinton, who joined consultancy Valliance last September after graduating from a Bachelor of Science in 2024, says the incorporation of AI into his role makes him feel less like a graduate, and more like an equal team member. He uses around 10 AI agents daily for different tasks.

"Your ideas and your creativity are a lot more valued because you actually get to implement those firsthand, and the responsibility you take on is a lot greater because of that," says London-based Clinton, 23.

"I am now taking on responsibilities which would usually take me four or five years to get to."

His career progression, he believes, will now be faster as a result.

"AI is killing the 'pyramid' approach…progression is no longer based on your knowledge bank. Now it's more based on your critical thinking and understanding of the processes," says Clinton.

There's no doubt Underwood, Patel and Clinton are developing valuable AI knowledge which can help them across their careers.

But with their time at work so focused on AI, does it matter how much - or how little - time they're spending learning about the professional field they're supposed to be operating in?

Underwood says she'd like to still pick up the traditional PR skills her role isn't currently focused on, but is confident of her future in the agency's growing AI team.

"There's certain things that I haven't had the chance to do yet, like directly pitching to the media. I absolutely plan to do this," she says.

Graduates becoming too AI-centric is an issue for Simon Pratt, chief operating officer at Portman Finance Group. He says being able to use AI effectively is important, but the company's two-year graduate programme is fully centred on "learning the trade".

"Our graduates rotate across four areas at six-month intervals, working directly alongside senior relationship managers to learn their trade," Northampton-based Pratt explains.

"They'll learn all of our financial products, how to draft credit papers for submission to lenders, and how to build meaningful relationships with our customers. They'll progress to running transactions from start to finish."

Claire Reed, PwC UK's chief technology and innovation officer, believes graduate roles that are too AI heavy won't necessarily provide graduates long-term career progression.

"There will be no graduate job now that doesn't require a baseline of AI literacy," says Glasgow-based Reed.

"But AI skills on their own are not going to help you in your career. You've got to couple that with that sector knowledge of what that client actually wants."

Back in Coventry, Dillan Patel is confident his AI work will continue to be valuable, and he wants to keep building on it.

"I don't think I'd want to explore different positions within the business. Through my involvement in AI-related projects, I already work closely with different areas of the business and I'm gaining valuable knowledge and experience along the way," he says.

articles.title: US Department of Justice expands its probe into Alaska’s US Senate election
articles.summary: The Trump administration is doubling down on allegations Democrats stood up a ‘spoiler’ candidate against Republicans.
articles.body:
The administration of United States President Donald Trump has stepped up its investigation into a US Senate race in the state of Alaska, where it says the Democratic Party put up a sham candidate to confuse voters so the Republican candidate would lose.

Federal prosecutors sent so-called “target” letters to a number of people on Tuesday, including attorney Marc Elias, who has represented the Democratic Party, warning them that it has gathered enough evidence linking them to a possible crime that it regards them as possible defendants in a future indictment.

In a statement on Tuesday, Elias said, “No one should be surprised that President Trump’s Department of Justice is targeting me and my law firm on Election Day.”

“We will not be intimidated by a sham investigation,” the statement continued. “We are going to keep working around the clock to support our clients and make sure President Trump and his party enjoy a well-deserved beating at the ballot box.”

Incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan is facing a midterm elections challenge from a former Democratic congresswoman, Mary Peltola, for a seat that could prove pivotal in determining which party controls the Senate.

One of the candidates in the race is also named Dan Sullivan, and Trump and officials in his administration have said the Democratic Party deliberately put the newcomer Sullivan up to running for office, to confuse voters on Election Day. Democrats have denied the accusations, and say that the ballots being used on Tuesday clearly mark each Sullivan separately.

But the Department of Justice, which unsuccessfully attempted to have a court block the certification of the election in the state if the incumbent Sullivan loses, has gone ahead with a sweeping investigation anyway.

The AP reported that more than 100 subpoenas had been sent out so far as part of the investigation, according to an unnamed person briefed on the probe.

articles.title: FBI arrests man for sending over 700 threatening letters to US officials
articles.summary: The suspect, an Oklahoma City man, is accused of mailing hoax letters with white powder and treason warnings.
articles.body:
A man from the Midwestern United States is facing federal charges after allegedly mailing hundreds of suspicious letters containing white powder and menacing warnings about treason ahead of the US midterm elections .

On Tuesday, Robin Patrick Martin, a 67-year-old Oklahoma City man, appeared for the first time in a US district court after his arrest a day earlier.

His charges include conveying false or misleading information or hoaxes, as well as mailing threatening communications.

Prosecutors have accused Martin of sending more than 700 letters containing a white powder to hundreds of state and federal officials, including members of the US Congress and election pollsters.

Initial testing showed the white powder was nonhazardous, consisting of yeast or flour, though not all the letters have been fully tested yet.

In an affidavit, Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) agent David Cole described the letters as expressing grievances about election integrity.

“The writer of the letter described perceived issues with the 2020 election, claimed that President Donald Trump won the 2020 election, and voiced concerns regarding some of the same issues recurring in the then-upcoming 2024 election,” said Cole.

The letters reportedly warned their recipients that they could face arrest for treason “or worse”.

“Stay on the right side of history! Your life may depend on it,” one letter read, in ink only visible through ultraviolet light, according to the FBI.

Trump, a Republican, has repeatedly cited false claims of election rigging to argue that he — not Democrat Joe Biden — won the 2020 presidential election.

Those false claims helped spur Trump’s supporters to storm the US Capitol on January 6, 2021, to disrupt the certification of the voting results.

Since being re-elected in 2024, Trump has continued to use his platform to spread fears of election fraud, which is considered exceedingly rare in the US.

The investigation that led to Martin’s arrest stretched back to 2024, when election officials in multiple states reported receiving mail containing a white substance.

The letters included a return address for the fictional “United States Traitor Elimination Army”, in Takoma Park, Maryland.

The FBI has said it gathered video footage of Martin visiting US Postal Service locations in Oklahoma City, Dallas and San Antonio, Texas, to send the mailings.

It also claims it has his fingerprints on a letter addressed to FBI Director Kash Patel.

The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) reportedly participated in the investigation after a suspect the FBI believes to be Martin sent messages to the group’s mailing list.

Those messages echoed the mailed letters, calling the DSA’s members traitors and accusing them of treason for voting in Tuesday’s midterm election.

articles.title: All's Fair: Why Kim Kardashian came back to 'the worst TV drama ever'
articles.summary: The media personality and businesswoman says she's worked on her acting for series two of All's Fair.
articles.body:
It was meant to be Kim Kardashian's triumphant debut as a leading actor - but last year's legal drama All's Fair was so universally panned by critics that it actually broke streaming records as audiences clambered to see what all the fuss was about.

Kardashian, who is best known as a media personality and businesswoman, tells the BBC she had no choice but to "lean into" the discourse and come back for a second series.

"We thought we were this law show, dealing with some really serious issues," she jokes.

But viewers mostly enjoyed its comedy value - with outlandish outfits and zingy one-liners from co-stars Sarah Paulson and Glenn Close sending the show straight into the pantheon of 'camp classics'.

'What choice do you have when you're getting criticised?'

"We're a full comedy now," the 46-year-old admits, adding: "The beauty in producing a show with writers that are really tuned in to pop culture is they can see what the response is and write accordingly to that."

All's Fair, which was created by American Horror Story and Glee showrunner Ryan Murphy, became the Hulu network's most-watched scripted series debut of the last three years and was immediately renewed.

Following a group of divorce lawyers - played by Kardashian, Close, Paulson, Naomi Watts and Niecy Nash-Betts - the show was panned for bad acting, with Kardashian baring the brunt of criticism.

The Hollywood Reporter called her "wooden", and the Times declared that the show "may be the worst TV drama ever".

But the hallmark of Kardashian's career has been her ability to back herself - whether that's going from years of being snubbed by Met Gala organisers to becoming its most anticipated guest, or overcoming backlash to the launch of her shapewear company to turn it into a $5bn (£3.7bn) brand .

Kardashian says: "What is the alternative, right? What is the other choice that you have when you're getting criticised?

"Do you just fall in and feel that, or keep your head down and try better, try harder and try a different path?"

Having been in the spotlight for more than 20 years, she's "always had a really good sense of my mental health", and says that comes from being able to "brush off" those who seek to bring her down.

"I always do things that are tough because I genuinely want to learn," Kardashian says.

While she was promoting the legal drama last year, Kardashian was waiting to find out if she had passed exams to become a lawyer in real life , after six years of studying for an apprenticeship that negated the need for a university degree.

Shortly after the first series aired, she found out she had failed the exam - but says that won't be the end of her pursuit of the qualification.

"If I don't pass something, if I don't do the best at something, then I'll get there," she says. "I don't worry. I just have to keep going."

But after her admission that she had used AI for legal advice , she does say she will change how public she is about her studies.

"I'm going to be a little more quiet about my journey until I get there," says Kardashian, who has four children with rapper Kanye West and is now in a relationship with British Formula 1 driver Lewis Hamilton.

"I know there was a lot of talk out there like, 'she's given up', and that's funny to me.

"I like people to think what they want to think and I'll take it again and let you guys know once I've passed. I'll be very vocal about that," she says.

'A realistic depiction of a lot of women'

Audiences have only been given a glimpse of what to expect from the second series of All's Fair so far.

Co-star Watts, who also serves as a producer on the show alongside Kardashian, says they have "doubled down" on "the high fashion, high drama and heightened reality" that audiences enjoyed the first time around.

"It doesn't mean that just because you're super smart that you can't be fashionable and into glamorous things as well," she adds.

articles.title: 50 years after Nepal banned cannabis, top court orders regulated cultivation
articles.summary: Fifty years after Nepal banned all cannabis cultivation, Supreme Court has directed govt to frame regulations within three months to allow its controlled
articles.body: Fifty years after Nepal banned all cannabis cultivation, Supreme Court has directed govt to frame regulations within three months to allow its controlled cultivation for medicinal, scientific and industrial purposes, potentially opening the door to a legal cannabis industry in the Himalayan nation. The court held that successive govts had failed to implement provisions of a law enacted in 1976 that already allowed limited cultivation under regulation.The verdict, delivered on May 18, 2025, remained unpublished for nearly 18 months after court records were destroyed during the violent Gen Z protests. Its full text emerged only last week, bringing attention to a ban Nepal imposed under international pressure.The court criticised successive govts for failing to implement provisions of the Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act, 1976, which permits certain forms of regulated cultivation and medicinal use."The failure to do so amounts to a refusal or neglect by govt to discharge its legal obligations," the court observed. The order did not permit recreational use, which remains illegal.Rajiv Kafle, a prominent cannabis legalisation campaigner, has long called for Nepal to replace prohibition with regulation. "In fact, regulation is a better policy option," he told TOI, pointing to the economic opportunities that countries with legal cannabis industries had already begun exploiting.How the ban came aboutDuring the 1960s and early 1970s, Kathmandu's Freak Street became a major stop on the hippie trail, drawing Western backpackers and Americans avoiding Vietnam War conscription. Govt-licensed shops openly sold marijuana and hashish, but pressure mounted on Nepal as then US President Richard Nixon intensified the 'War on Drugs'.Nepal revoked cannabis trading licences in 1973.The Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act, 1976, later criminalised cultivation, sale and consumption, while retaining limited regulated exceptions that successive govts failed to implement. articles.title: Fears for ancient woodlands as pressure grows to build more homes
articles.summary: Dozens of individual sites feature planned developments immediately next to woods, the BBC finds.
articles.body:
Ancient woodland campaigners fear a drive to build more houses could put some of England's oldest habitats under increasing pressure, despite government protections designed to prevent their loss.

The protected areas can only be built on or near in "wholly exceptional circumstances", according to planning policy.

But the Labour government's pledge to build 1.5 million new homes by the end of 2029 and the recent creation of the "grey belt" - areas of poorer quality open spaces that can be built on - are leaving ancient woodlands at threat, campaigners say.

A spokesman for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said ancient woodlands continued to benefit from "very clear and strong protections".

But the BBC has found dozens of individual sites which feature planned developments immediately next to the woods.

Among them are approved plans for 450 homes within yards of Hook Wood in Gillingham, Kent, which residents fear will have a devastating impact on local wildlife.

"We are already seeing cases where the existing protections are struggling," said Ancient Woodland UK chairwoman Lucy Graebe-Watson.

"We have seen a rise in concerns and alerts from local groups since recent planning reforms."

An ancient woodland is classed as existing continuously since at least the year 1600. The sites, described as "irreplaceable by Graebe-Watson, are considered some of the UK's richest habitats for wildlife.

The National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) , external guidelines for local councils deciding planning applications in England say woods can be built on in "wholly exceptional circumstances", such as major infrastructure projects like HS2.

But Graebe-Watson said the grey belt policy made it more likely areas directly next to ancient woodland - previously protected under green belt laws - could be developed.

In the East Midlands, the growing demand for housing is raising concerns about development proposals on land bordering Chaddesden Wood Nature Reserve in Derby.

Helen Cherry, who has lived nearby for 40 years, is among more than 1,500 people objecting to plans for about 150 houses there.

"The wood is at least 400 years old, with mature hazel and oak trees," said the former cafe owner, who regularly walks her dog there.

She said building to the edge of the ancient woodland would leave the site "closed on all sides", making a "mockery" of the nature reserve and undermining its protected status.

"Many a day I've been brought to tears, stopped and looked across the field where the buildings may occur and you can see right out across to the Derbyshire Dales," she added.

"It's absolutely beautiful. If houses went ahead, the view would be completely obliterated - it would be very sad."

Derby City Council refused the plans in 2025, but surveyors were seen at the site over the summer. People living near the site said they feared developers JGP Properties Limited would come back with amended proposals.

JGP Properties told the Local Democracy Reporting Service its assessments demonstrated "no loss or deterioration of the ancient woodland and veteran trees".

The Royal Society for the Protection of Birds said protections for irreplaceable habitats had improved under the recent changes to the NPPF.

However, Carl Bunnage, head of nature policy for the charity, said they remained inadequate.

He argued allowing development in "wholly exceptional circumstances" represented a loophole for developers, especially in areas with a shortage of houses.

He said planning reforms were in favour of development, with housing and economic growth policies often carrying greater weight than nature conservation.

"If we can give the strongest protections to built heritage features such as historic buildings, then why shouldn't we also be giving the strongest protections to those habitats?" Bunnage said.

In South Yorkshire, concerns are being raised over the impact of a 130-home development on land surrounding Gelster Wood.

It has sparked a campaign in the village of Rossington, near Doncaster, with residents worried the proposal could permanently alter a centuries-old landscape.

More than 2,000 people have backed efforts to challenge the plans.

"People feel our village is being treated as an easy target for developers who don't care about our community or our heritage," said Gary Cantrill, a local beekeeper and member of the Preserve Littleworth Lane Group.

"This isn't just an empty plot. It's 350-year-old historic farmland."

He said residents were also worried about flooding as the fields currently absorbed "vast amounts of rainwater".

"Concreting over this land replaces natural drainage and creates a huge risk of flooding into neighbouring properties and roads," he added.

Matt Shardlow, an ecological consultant working with the campaign, said damage could be caused to ancient woodlands, even when trees were not removed.

Roots extending away from the sites could be damaged by development, he said, while drainage for nearby new housing could dry out certain tree species and pollute their water supplies.

Noise and light pollution could also drive sensitive species out of the woods, Shardlow added. Even having pet cats in an area could affect populations of ground-nesting birds, bats and other species, he said.

A spokesperson for developers Albemarle Homes said the woodland itself was not included in the original site and any future plans would have to comply with environmental rules.

A spokesman for the government's housing department said national planning rules "explicitly" stated developments that would cause the loss or deterioration of ancient woodland should be refused.

He added there were "very limited exceptions" to the policy, limited to some nationally significant infrastructure projects. He added in those cases compensation measures would be required.

The department said a revised NPPF published in August contained clearer policies for assessing development proposals affecting irreplaceable habitats.

articles.title: UN elects five judges to International Court of Justice amid record cases
articles.summary: The election, held at UN headquarters, required several rounds of voting to fill the fifth and final seat.
articles.body:
The United Nations has elected five judges to the International Court of Justice (ICJ) for nine-year terms, as the court faces a record caseload, including South Africa’s genocide case against Israel over its war on Gaza.

The vote was held on Tuesday at UN headquarters, with candidates requiring an absolute majority in both the General Assembly and the Security Council to win.

Dapo Akande of the United Kingdom, Francois Alabrune of France, Mahmoud Daifallah Hmoud of Jordan, Rena Lee of Singapore and Phoebe Okowa of Kenya were elected to the 15-member panel.

Their terms are set to begin on February 6, 2027.

The two UN bodies initially agreed on four candidates but failed to select a fifth. The Security Council supported Ecuador’s Marcelo Vazquez-Bermudez, while the General Assembly backed Okowa, prompting further rounds of voting.

Vazquez-Bermudez later withdrew from the race, and Okowa subsequently won the backing of the General Assembly and the Security Council.

The votes were held by secret ballot concurrently, but separately.

The ICJ is based in The Hague and has 15 judges, each from a different country. They serve nine-year terms and may be re-elected. To ensure a degree of continuity, a third of the bench is elected every three years.

The election comes as the World Court faces a record workload.

ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa told the General Assembly on October 29 that 24 contentious cases are pending, covering disputes over territory, human rights and the interpretation of international treaties.

Among them is South Africa’s case accusing Israel of violating the Genocide Convention in its war on Gaza. The court has previously ordered provisional measures but has not issued a final ruling on whether genocide occurred.

In October 2025, the court issued an advisory opinion outlining Israel’s obligations towards the UN and humanitarian organisations operating in the occupied Palestinian territory.

Separately, the court announced on Tuesday that it would deliver a judgment on November 19 in The Gambia’s case accusing Myanmar of genocide against the Rohingya minority.

Established in 1945, the ICJ is the UN’s principal judicial organ, responsible for settling disputes between states and providing advisory opinions on questions of international law.

articles.title: US midterms: Indian-origin Suhas Subramanyam wins re-election to US House from Virginia
articles.summary: Indian-origin Democrat Suhas Subramanyam has won re-election to the US House of Representatives from Virginia's 10th Congressional District in the 2026
articles.body: Indian-origin Democrat Suhas Subramanyam has won re-election to the US House of Representatives from Virginia's 10th Congressional District in the 2026 midterm elections, defeating Republican challenger Dave T Beckwith.Subramanyam secured 63.16% of the vote, polling 1,73,106 votes, while Beckwith received 34.66%, or 94,990 votes. Independent candidate Ahsen Mujeeb Malik finished third with 1.99% (5,444 votes), while write-in candidates accounted for the remaining 0.19%.The victory comes after Subramanyam urged Indian-Americans to participate actively in the midterm elections, saying their votes and voices mattered more than ever amid rising hate and discrimination in the US. Speaking to ANI after voting at a polling station in Manassas, Virginia, on Tuesday, he said the state was witnessing record turnout and expressed confidence about the Democrats' prospects."Well, come out and vote. Make your voice heard. Your vote matters more than ever, especially at a time when we're seeing record hate in our community, in our country," he said.Encouraging Indian-Americans to consider entering politics, Subramanyam drew from his own experience of contesting and winning elections. "I ran for office and I won. You can too. If you want to get involved in the political process, now is the time. It's more important than ever," he added.The Congressman also criticised the functioning of the US Congress, saying people were dissatisfied with representatives who prioritised the President over ordinary citizens. He said Democrats would focus on restoring healthcare and food assistance and ensuring public resources benefited Americans.Born in Virginia in 1979 to Indian immigrant parents, Subramanyam is the first Indian-American to represent the state's 10th Congressional District. He previously served as a technology policy adviser in the White House under former President Barack Obama before entering politics.Subramanyam was elected to the Virginia House of Delegates in 2019 and subsequently served in the state Senate from 2023 to 2024. He entered the US House in 2024, succeeding retiring Democratic representative Jennifer Wexton.During his campaign, he criticised President Donald Trump's administration over rising costs, healthcare concerns and its treatment of the federal workforce. articles.title: 'Aren't we secular?' HC asks BMC to restore actor Dia Mirza's anti-cracker post
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Bombay HC said it's \"unfortunate\" BMC had removed from its social media pages a video of actor Dia Mirza urging citizens to avoid crackers as part
articles.body: MUMBAI: Bombay HC said it's "unfortunate" BMC had removed from its social media pages a video of actor Dia Mirza urging citizens to avoid crackers as part of the anti-pollution drive. It suggested the post be "put back" to restore people's confidence, reports Rosy Sequeira.HC said it was "disturbed by comments in regard to celebrities who had participated and assisted in public cause". It further said, "There could not have been any other colour which could be given, and more particularly, when there are court directions." It asked, "How do you object to a person's participation? Are we not a secular country?"Celebrities were roped in for BMC’s campaign against firecrackers after HC’s nudge last week. Pointing out that it was “really upset” over actor Dia Mirza’s post being removed, Justices Girish Kulkarni and Neela Gokhale said, “We would desire that in the event any goodwill message of any celebrity was taken off from the corporation’s social media, it would be ideal if the same is put back in the spirit of what Supreme Court observed that the festival is for everybody to celebrate.”Justice Kulkarni said they didn’t approve of BMC’s move. “Somebody is voluntarily coming forward, who has always been associated with social causes, and you are going to reprimand that person. With all this petty-mindedness.”The judges said Mirza “had rendered a very very good message in terms of environment, noise pollution and air pollution”. “There was nothing. There was no question of objection. No question of giving any colour. Most unfortunate,” said Justice Kulkarni.HC suggested that BMC reupload the video. “...it should not have been taken off... please put it again and restore the confidence of the people in the Constitution and society... This is a constitutional requirement, not this kind of thought. And these are stray thoughts of one or two persons,” said Justice KulkarniHC said environment, air and noise pollution are of paramount concerns, and every person can canvass and “bring this sensitisation to the public fore”. “Therefore, [asking] why X person was picked up etc is not a good thing,” said Justice Kulkarni.Hearing a suo motu PIL on festival noise and air pollution due to firecrackers, HC had on Oct 26 said it expected celebrities to voluntarily come forward to spread awareness. On Tuesday, the judges told BMC’s advocate Joel Carlos to congratulate civic chief Ashwini Bhide for the “impeccable steps she has taken”, particularly by getting celebrities to spread awareness. State’s advocate Jyoti Chavan said the HC order had created so much goodwill that celebrities “suo motu approached us”.The bench cited Supreme Court’s Monday order that Diwali is a national festival and also referred to raising of awareness by celebrities. It asked whether SC and HC orders have any qualification.The judges said their order seeking measures to keep the bursting of firecrackers in check wasn’t just for Diwali but also for “all 365 days”. articles.title: Killer who escaped Tennessee prison captured after week-long manhunt
articles.summary: Jacob Allen Morley was serving a life sentence for murder before he escaped over a prison fence.
articles.body:
US authorities have recaptured a convicted murderer who escaped a Tennessee prison more than a week ago.

Jacob Allen Morley, 28, was serving a life sentence over the killing of his colleague in 2022, when he escaped from the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville, about 90 miles (145 km) north of Memphis.

The Tennessee Department of Correction (TDOC) said security footage showed Morley, wearing his prison uniform, breaching the prison fence around 11:30pm on 25 October, and later stealing a vehicle from a nearby farm.

On Wednesday the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation (TBI) announced Morley was in custody after an operation that involved local, state and federal agencies.

In a statement, the TBI said authorities had received a tip that Morley was hiding on an Illinois property, from which a truck had also been stolen.

The truck's licence plate was then tracked through automatic plate-reader technology, travelling through Missouri, where local authorities were dispatched to follow.

Morley was apprehended by Missouri State Highway Patrol "without incident" in Carroll County at 11:34am local time on Tuesday. Three firearms that had previously been reported stolen were also recovered from the vehicle, the TBI said.

Photos published by authorities showed Morley handcuffed and being led out of a field by officers.

Following his escape, Morley had been added to the TBI's most wanted list, with the TDOC offering a reward of up to $2,500 (£1,900) for information leading to his arrest. The reward was increased by $15,000 on Wednesday.

The TBI's statement said members of the public had provided information during the investigation, but did not say if the reward had been paid.

The Missouri State Highway Patrol said the manhunt had involved officers from the Kansas City Police Department, Independence Police Department, the FBI, US Marshals Service and Homeland Security Investigations.

Morley was convicted of first-degree murder over the death of his colleague Cody Birchfield in 2022. He was sentenced in June 2025. His request for a new trial was denied in May.

Birchfield's body was found in a metal box under Morley's home, according to Carter County court records reviewed by the BBC.

Birchfield died "as a result of a gunshot wound to the back of the head", a pathology report cited in court said. Bullet casings matched a gun found in Morley's house.

Birchfield's sister said in her victim impact statement to the court that the pair had developed a friendship while Birchfield was training Morley at the pallet manufacturing company where they were both employed.

Besides murder, Morley was also convicted of vandalism, tampering with evidence, aggravated burglary, and evading arrest.

This is not the first time Morley has led law enforcement officials on a manhunt. His 2022 arrest came after a police chase that crossed state lines into North Carolina.

The Northwest Correctional Complex is a men's prison with the capacity to hold up to 1,776 inmates, from low security to maximum, the BBC's partner CBS reported.

CBS said the prison has seen numerous acts of violence in recent years, and in July a grand jury returned dozens of indictments over assaults on staff and the murders of five inmates.

articles.title: Spain’s transport minister steps down 6 days after fatal high-speed rail crash
articles.summary: MADRID — Spain’s Transport Minister Óscar Puente announced Tuesday that he is stepping down, six days after a high-speed train collision south of Madrid killed 69 people.
articles.body: MADRID — Spain’s Transport Minister Óscar Puente announced Tuesday that he is stepping down, six days after a high-speed train collision south of Madrid killed 69 people. He made the announcement at the end of an hourslong appearance before lawmakers about the crash — the second such deadly collision this year involving Spain’s extensive high-speed rail network. “A transport minister in a country like Spain cannot remain in office after two accidents of this seriousness in less than a year,” Puente said. The Oct. 28 crash took place when a high-speed train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks. The chain of events that led to disaster started when the communication system key to the functioning of the security system on the Madrid-Seville line went down. Central controllers in Madrid took over and gave the go-ahead for a state-operated Renfe high-speed train to proceed, even though there was a stationary train ahead operated by the company Iryo. It was the second major crash on the Madrid-Seville line this year. In January, more than two hours further south along the route, a train derailed and struck another traveling in the opposite direction, killing 46 people. That crash remains under investigation. Puente said he had taken the decision to resign immediately after the deadly crash, but had not made it public. The collisions have raised fresh concerns about the safety of the country’s rail network, and the most recent crash came four weeks before a national election. Spain’s high-speed rail network has been considered one of the country’s crowning achievements. It is the world’s second-largest, after China’s. Until this year, it had not experienced a deadly crash since coming into service over three decades ago. Earlier Tuesday, Puente announced safety measures the government would implement on the rail network, including improving conditions in control centers and pushing for a faster rollout of the standardized European Rail Traffic Management System for safety and signaling.

articles.title: Teen previously convicted in shooting accused of killing pregnant mom of 4 inside Spirit Halloween
articles.summary: Monte Smith, 17, allegedly opened fire inside a Spirit Halloween store at Solano Town Center, killing pregnant mother Constance Hages and wounding six.
articles.body: A California teen released after a prior shooting arrest is now accused of gunning down a pregnant mother of four at a Spirit Halloween store, prompting prosecutors to push to try the 17-year-old as an adult. Monte Smith was arrested Nov. 2 after the attack at Fairfield’s Solano Town Center left Constance Hages, 31, dead and six others wounded, according to Fairfield police. The Solano County District Attorney’s Office has also charged him with two counts of murder and asked a judge to move his case to adult court. CALIFORNIA GUNMAN REPEATEDLY RELEASED BEFORE DEADLY RAMPAGE, FIERY SHOOTOUT WITH DEPUTIES Smith had already been arrested in another shooting before the deadly attack at Spirit Halloween, according to Fairfield police. That case involved gunfire in a local high school parking lot after school hours in 2025. He received a sentence and was later released, the department said. "It’s time for change in California," Fairfield Police Chief Dan Marshall said, according to KTVU. "I don’t know how many more people have to die at the hands of youth. Hopefully we’ve had plenty enough." MARYLAND MAN ACCUSED OF GIRL'S FATAL SHOOTING RELEASED FROM PRISON DAYS BEFORE Prosecutors also pointed to Smith’s record in explaining why they want him kept in custody. "Due to the seriousness of these crimes, the minor’s criminal record, and the threat to public safety, the people will argue that Smith remain detained," the DA’s office said. TWO TEEN SUSPECTS HELD AFTER 5 FAMILY MEMBERS KILLED IN 'TARGETED MASS SHOOTING' The filing also alleges a prior violent offense conviction, described as a strike, though the DA’s announcement did not specify the underlying offense. Hages’ death has left four children without their mother, according to a GoFundMe organized by her aunt, Clanisha Morton. Police confirmed Hages was pregnant when she was killed. "Constance was deeply loved, and her absence has created an overwhelming void in the lives of everyone who knew and cherished her," Morton wrote. The family is raising money for funeral expenses and care for her children. 15-YEAR-OLD ACCUSED OF FIRING INTO CROWD DURING DEADLY SEATTLE MASS SHOOTING CLAIMS SELF-DEFENSE The gunfire erupted around 8:30 p.m. Oct. 30, after Smith allegedly walked into the store and spotted another customer whom investigators believe he intended to target, police said. He pulled out a gun and fired multiple rounds, striking that person and six others, according to police. Hages died at the scene. Investigators have not identified the intended target or said what led to the shooting. Smith fled within minutes, just as officers arrived, police said. As first responders treated the wounded, a school resource officer helped investigators identify the suspect. The officer recognized Smith as a former student while reviewing surveillance video from the store and immediately alerted detectives, according to police. That recognition helped identify him within hours of the initial 911 call, and detectives ultimately located him at a residence in neighboring Suisun City. Police initially withheld Smith’s name because of his age. The DA’s office later publicly identified him in its charging announcement. CALIFORNIA HIGH SCHOOL GRADUATION SHOOTING KILLS TEEN, INJURES CHILD AND TWO OTHERS The FBI also assisted with the investigation, confirming to Fox News Digital that its Evidence Response Team helped Fairfield police process a portion of the crime scene. In addition to the two murder counts, Smith faces three counts of attempted murder, three counts of assault with a semiautomatic weapon and multiple gun enhancements, according to the DA’s office. Prosecutors also filed a multiple-murder special circumstance allegation. The office announced that Smith’s arraignment and detention hearing was scheduled for Nov. 4 at 9 a.m. Its request to prosecute him as an adult requires a judge’s approval. Police have not identified the school involved in the earlier shooting or said when Smith was released in that case. In an update Saturday about the surviving victims, police said a 16-year-old boy, a 19-year-old man and a 32-year-old man were in critical condition, while a 23-year-old man was in critical but stable condition. Two other men, ages 19 and 43, had been treated for gunshot wounds and released. The department’s arrest announcement did not provide updated conditions. "The criminal justice process will now move forward, and we remain committed to ensuring accountability for the lives impacted by this senseless act of violence." Anyone with information about the shooting is asked to contact Fairfield police at 707-428-7600 or email 1030mall@fairfield.ca.gov.

articles.title: Keisha Lance Bottoms makes history as first Black woman elected US governor
articles.summary: Bottoms, a former adviser to former President Joe Biden, beat Republican Rick Jackson to win the Georgia governor’s race
articles.body:
Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms has made history as the first Black woman elected governor of a US state, according to Associated Press news agency projections.

The former Atlanta mayor emerged victorious in Georgia over her billionaire opponent, Republican Rick Jackson, who spent more than $200m of his personal fortune in an attempt to succeed the popular outgoing Republican governor, Brian Kemp.

Bottoms, a former adviser to US President Joe Biden, was propelled to victory in part by the state’s significant Black voting bloc, which turned out in large numbers during early voting.

During the campaign, she faced Republican attempts to characterise her time as mayor as a crime-ridden decline for the state’s largest city.

“It’s a longstanding playbook to paint Atlanta as this big bad place,” Bottoms told the Associated Press news agency.

Bottoms’ win marks the third consecutive time that Georgia Democrats have nominated a Black woman for governor. Stacey Abrams lost in 2018 and 2022 to Kemp, who is leaving office in January after eight years due to term limits.

articles.title: EU urges action as Germany, Romania and UK report supermarket cyberattacks
articles.summary: EU says supermarket hacks in at least 11 countries are ‘not isolated’, but a Romanian official suspects no state actor.
articles.body:
Hackers raised the temperatures of refrigeration systems at supermarkets in Germany, Romania and the United Kingdom during Monday’s cyberattacks , officials said, bringing the number of European countries affected in the hacking spree to at least 11.

The announcements on Tuesday came as the European Union promised a collective response, warning that the attacks, which have spoiled tonnes of food across the continent, were “not isolated”.

The motive for the cyberattacks is unknown, and no one has claimed responsibility. A Romanian official said he did not suspect a state actor.

Problems were reported in at least nine EU countries on Monday: Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal and Sweden. On Tuesday, officials and company representatives said four supermarkets in Germany and six in Romania were affected.

The UK, which is not in the EU, was also hit.

Thomas Regnier, a spokesperson for the EU, said the bloc’s agencies were talking with national authorities to develop a joint response.

“These are not isolated incidents, and of course, we have to be collectively resilient and prepared for such cyber incidents,” he said.

But he refused to point the finger at any potential culprits.

Romania’s top cybersecurity official played down the threat.

“It seems semi-amateurish,” Dan Cimpean, the director of Romania’s National Cyber Security Directorate, told the AFP news agency. “We do not suspect, under any circumstances, that it is a state actor.”

He added that “no other infrastructure was compromised”.

Belgium was among the hardest-hit countries on Monday, with dozens of stores across several grocery chains reporting refrigeration failures. Federal prosecutors there have opened an investigation.

In Italy, about 20 supermarkets were affected.

Giuseppe Spadaro, director of a group that runs Coop supermarkets in Sicily, said four of its 300 stores were hit, causing thousands of euros in damage.

“We had to throw away everything. The shelves are empty,” he told Italy’s Corriere della Sera newspaper.

Italy’s government held talks with the heads of the intelligence services and the National Cybersecurity Agency on Tuesday after the attacks, and Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s office said the incident had a “limited” impact.

“There is no cause for alarm, although all the relevant institutional bodies remain on high alert,” it said in a statement.

In the UK, hackers tried to target small meat-processing firms, but the impact was minimal, said Richard Horne, chief executive of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC).

Horne told the BBC the issue affected “the whole food supply chain”, and that there had been a couple of instances where “vulnerable technology had been exploited”.

The second wave of attacks mirrored the cyberattack that swept hundreds of supermarkets across France in October, which also affected stores in several other European countries.

In Sweden, the supermarket chain Coop said that refrigerators and freezers affected overnight at seven of its stores had been connected to “old 4G networks”, and that the stores had since resumed normal operations.

Carlos Cancinos, a spokesperson for the chain, said Coop had accelerated an upgrade, begun after the October attacks, to move its connected refrigeration equipment onto 5G networks and modern modems.

“This helps to solve a large share of problems of this kind,” he said.

Danfoss, a Danish maker of refrigeration controls whose systems were again among those targeted, said it had been in close contact with customers for the past three weeks. It recommended that the systems not be directly accessible from the internet.

Frank Groenewegen, a cybersecurity expert at Deloitte in The Hague, urged retailers to check whether their refrigeration controllers were connected to the internet and running the latest security updates.

“And if they don’t even know, then remove them from the public internet immediately,” he told the Reuters news agency. “With disconnecting, you haven’t fixed the root cause, but you’ve at least isolated those systems so that an attacker is not able to do this anymore.”

articles.title: South Carolina elects Democratic senator for first time in almost three decades
articles.summary: Annie Andrews is projected to defeat Darline Graham, who was handpicked by President Trump to take her brother's seat after his death.
articles.body:
Republican South Carolina Senate candidate Darline Graham is projected to have lost her race, handing Democrats their first victory in the state for 28 years.

Democrat Annie Andrews, a former paediatrician, was on course to pull off a stunning upset in Tuesday's midterm elections, according to the BBC's US partner CBS.

Graham was appointed to fill the seat in July after the sudden death of her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham, a move that won support from President Donald Trump.

A political newcomer, she conceded during the primary that she was "not that informed on national security".

Trump won the state by 18 points in 2024.

During her primary campaign, Graham acknowledged her lack of political experience, particularly after stumbling on a foreign policy question during a recent debate.

Asked about the US stance towards Taiwan, Graham had said: "National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise, but I do support the military."

Her brother, Lindsey Graham, was elected to the Senate in 2002 and was one of Washington's most influential voices on foreign policy, often pushing for US military intervention overseas.

articles.title: Hillary Clinton warns Dems may squander midterm victory if they fail to stay focused after election
articles.summary: Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton laid out a three-part Democratic agenda after the midterms covering affordability, anti-corruption and DOGE.
articles.body: Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton warned on the "Pivot" podcast that even if Democrats score major victories in the midterms, they could squander their gains if they fail to focus on the issues that matter to voters most. Clinton spoke with "Pivot" podcast co-hosts Kara Swisher and Scott Galloway at a live Election Night event and predicted a Democratic wave. "I think we're going to wake up to a Democratic House and a Democratic Senate," she told the co-hosts. Galloway agreed with Clinton's prediction but warned that it may be a short-term victory if Democrats do not respond to voter concerns. BILL AND HILLARY CLINTON MAKE ELEVENTH-HOUR MIDTERM MOVES AS PARTY'S OLD GUARD FACES NEW REALITY "Let's count our chickens and assume we take the House and the Senate, and it's Nov. 4. I would argue it's a lease, not a mortgage; dating, not a relationship," Galloway said. "I think that it'll be a function of not them loving Democrats, but hating us less. "What do you think the Democratic Party needs to do, or Democratic leadership, what are two or three things you think they need to do immediately such that we can turn this into something enduring going into ‘28 instead of just them flipping back in 24 months?" Clinton agreed, warning that Democrats would need to capitalize on any midterm victories and follow through on their agenda if they want to win in 2028 as well. "You're absolutely right, Scott. If the Democrats don't go in with an agenda and have the discipline to enact that agenda, then they're going to lose the kind of support that they're going to gain in this election," she said. TIM WALZ WARNS DEMOCRATS WILL FACE RECKONING IF THEY WIN POWER AND FAIL TO DELIVER CHANGE Clinton said Democrats could capitalize on potential midterm victories by focusing on affordability, corruption and investigations into the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE). "Number one, they ought to look at the affordability agenda. What's going to be in that? I think there are several things, one of which is healthcare costs," Clinton said. "But there also can be even more fast-tracking of, you know, housing starts, taking a hard look at how we can, you know, shift the burden on fossil fuel costs from consumers to the oil and gas companies which have recorded record profits. "So, I think that there's a lot of good work being done right now to put together an affordability package. "Secondly, an anti-corruption package. You know, people have to feel that this issue of corruption is going to be front and center because it has been costing money," she said. "People have been benefiting at the expense of, you know, everyday Americans, consumers, people who get up every day and try to make a living." The final step, she said, would be to do some investigations into DOGE's impact.
