articles.title: Federal judge temporarily blocks Trump plan to deport detained Afghans to Afghanistan
articles.summary: The order, which expires Saturday, forbids ICE to deport Afghan nationals to Pakistan or Taliban-ruled Afghanistan, which critics say could put their lives at risk.
articles.body: MIAMI — A federal judge on Tuesday temporarily blocked the Trump administration’s plans to deport Afghans detained in the United States to Afghanistan or Pakistan, after advocates and dozens of members of Congress warned that their lives would be at risk. The government told the court that Immigration and Customs Enforcement had no chartered or commercial flights for deporting Afghan nationals to Afghanistan or Pakistan at least before the end of the week. Judge Valerie Caproni’s order, which expires Saturday, asks all officials to adhere to that. ICE books the flights weeks in advance. A letter led by California Democratic Rep. Scott Peters and signed by 65 other members of the House and Senate said they were “extremely concerned that sending vulnerable people” would expose them to “persecution, torture, or even death.” The letter was sent Monday to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. Immigrant rights organizations have also warned that those deported could face retaliation from the Taliban. Thousands of Afghans fled persecution and feared for their lives after helping the U.S. military and aid groups in Afghanistan. According to court documents obtained by The Associated Press, the U.S. planned to deport Afghan immigrants on Monday on flights from Louisiana, where ICE has immigrant detention and processing facilities, to Pakistan. President Donald Trump’s administration has deported thousands of immigrants to countries other than their own. In some cases, it has resorted to third-country deportations when removal to their countries of origin was not possible, like when formal diplomatic relations were absent, as is the case with Afghanistan’s Taliban government. In other instances, third-country deportations have been used as a deterrent. Advocates and attorneys said that more than 80 detained Afghans had contacted them after ICE notified them that they could be deported this week via Pakistan. Among them are women, a police officer, members of religious minorities and people whose family members served in the U.S. military. Most fled Afghanistan because of persecution and do not have legal representation, according to Human Rights First and AfghanEvac, a nonprofit organization that advocates for immigrants. Before the judge signed her order, Zia Ahmad Takal, deputy spokesperson for the Afghan foreign ministry, said “the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan expresses its serious concern” about the reports that the U.S. plans to transfer Afghans to Pakistan. Takal called on the U.S. to make sure that decisions or actions are based on rights and “legitimate demands” of those involved, and said “third-party countries should not engage in dealings concerning the fate of another nation’s citizens.” “Today is a good day,” Shawn VanDiver, president at AfghanEvac, said at a news conference. “But I want to be honest with you, this is a reprieve, not a resolution. We haven’t stopped this fight forever. This is just a pause.” Savitri Arvey, director of policy, refugee and immigrant rights for Human Rights First, said individuals returned to Afghanistan “face grave, systematic dangers,” including arbitrary detentions, executions, public flogging and retaliatory violence. “The stakes were very, very high,” she said, noting that women and girls face severe restrictions in Afghanistan, including systematic denials of education, employment and public speech. Advocates expressed their concern about the role of the Pakistani government in facilitating the returns to Afghanistan and the fact that there is no information about the arrangements that the U.S. has made with Pakistan. “We celebrate today, but we’re getting right back to work tomorrow, continuing to make sure through our flight tracking that none of these flights are taking off,” Arvey said.

articles.title: Democrat Annie Andrews flips South Carolina’s Senate seat
articles.summary: Andrews beats Republican incumbent Darline Graham, sister of the late Senator Lindsey Graham, in a major upset.
articles.body:
Charleston, South Carolina, US – South Carolina has elected a Democrat to the US Senate for the first time since 1998, according to the Associated Press news agency. In a major upset for the Republican Party, Annie Andrews won in a state seen as a solid Republican stronghold.

“I think we just made some history,” Andrews said on Tuesday night after results came in.

Andrews outraised Republican candidate Darline Graham by more than $22m, according to Federal Election Commission filings, primarily with grassroots donations. She had pledged to take no money from corporate political action committees (PACs).

Andrews campaigned on lowering costs for working families, expanding affordable healthcare and protecting reproductive rights, and on opposing endless wars.

Despite South Carolina being reliably conservative, many voters, including Republicans, believed Graham to be unqualified.

After Republican Senator Lindsey Graham died suddenly in July, his younger sister, Darline, was appointed to serve out the remainder of his term. She went on to win a special primary runoff for the Republican nomination with US President Donald Trump’s endorsement.

Despite Trump’s endorsement, Graham struggled to unite conservatives behind her candidacy. During a primary debate, she said she was “not that informed on national security” and that “national security is not my thing”.

In the final month of the campaign, Trump made multiple appearances alongside Graham, an unusual investment of presidential time in a state Republicans normally win comfortably.

On Tuesday night, Andrews said Graham had called her and congratulated her on her win, which Andrews said she thanked her for.

In a victory speech, Andrews said, “This Senate seat doesn’t belong to one family, one party, or to Washington, DC. It belongs to you and it always will.”

“Nobody in Washington recruited me to run. Nobody handed me a seat in the United States Senate. And nobody wrote me a script,” Andrews said. “I owe no one in Washington anything.”

What does the win mean for South Carolina?

A South Carolina motto is, “While I breathe, I hope”. It appears on the right side of the South Carolina state seal. Many invoked this phrase as the results came in, claiming that this was their moment of hope

A group of medical students who attend the same medical school as Andrews were celebrating her win at the election watch party. They also volunteer at the free clinic in Mount Pleasant that provides free healthcare to uninsured people.

“Having a scientist in that space means a lot to us,” Daniel Newlands, one of the students, told Al Jazeera.

Lela Ali, a regional voting advisor in the South, told Al Jazeera that Andrews’s win could signal a change not only in South Carolina, but also for southern states.

“I think this victory and the gains across the region today gives people across the South a renewed sense of possibility,” Ali said. “We can’t turn our backs on the South.”

Toni Reale, 48, a mother and small business owner, teared up after Andrews win.

“In order for Annie to win, people would have had to change their typical votes, and that, to me, signals that people in my community have really thought about the options and put South Carolina first,” she told Al Jazeera.

She added, “We have a very smart and very hard-working electorate here in the state. And some really salt of the earth people that often vote against their best interests. And today, what I saw is people not just voting along party lines, but actually thinking about what’s best for our state.”

Holly Griffin, a 52-year-old healthcare worker, told Al Jazeera that the results show things are different for the state now.

“I think this shows the whole community that we have changed in front of us,” she said.

articles.title: China disputes reports of artillery shell found in Papua New Guinea
articles.summary: Papua New Guinea police had earlier dismissed speculation that the 32kg object was "merely a dummy".
articles.body:
Chinese authorities have dismissed reports that a suspected China-made artillery shell was found in a commercial shipping container in Papua New Guinea, saying it is a "shell-shaped wine bottle".

"It poses no danger at all," the Chinese embassy wrote in a Facebook post on Tuesday, drawing skeptical comments.

Police in Port Moresby arrested four Chinese nationals last Friday after the 32kg object was found at a construction site in the capital city.

Authorities were looking into whether it was a live device, local reports said then, with police commissioner David Manning describing it as "a very concerning discovery".

In a report on Wednesday, the Australia Broadcasting Corporation cited unnamed sources identifying the object as an undetonated 130mm Chinese Type 59 Artillery Projectile that contains chemical explosives and a fuse. The BBC has not independently verified this.

Papua New Guinea police had earlier dismissed speculation that the object was "merely a dummy", local newspaper Post Courier said.

However, the Chinese embassy said in its statement that it is "virtually impossible" for an illegal military-grade artillery shell to be smuggled out of China to Papua New Guinea.

"China enforces some of the world's strictest firearm control laws and regulations," it wrote, adding that China is "widely recognised as one of the safest countries globally".

"What sort of wine bottle weighs 32 kilograms?" wrote one of them.

Another wrote that the object bore no labels indicating that it's a wine bottle.

articles.title: Talarico wins Senate race, ending decades of Republican dominance in Texas
articles.summary: Democrats celebrate Talarico’s and Hinojosa’s victories, redefining Texas politics after decades of Republican reign.
articles.body:
Houston, Texas – James Talarico has won the United States Senate race in Texas, the first time a Democrat has won state office since 1994.

Tuesday’s victory marks a seismic shift in Texas , which has become a standard-bearer for the Republican Party’s staunch conservative policies.

“We just took back Texas,” Talarico said during a victory speech in Austin. “We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas.”

“We just showed that a politics of division is no match for a politics of love,” he said. “And we just sent a message to every billionaire mega donor, every trillionaire mega donor, every corrupt defender of this broken political system in this state, in this country – power belongs to the people.”

The win comes after an intervention in the Republican primary by President Donald Trump, who endorsed scandal-ridden Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton over incumbent John Cornyn.

But Paxton failed to generate enthusiasm, even among his party, despite record-breaking spending topping half a billion dollars.

The largest share came from trillionaire donor Elon Musk, who spent at least $212m supporting Paxton.

Musk’s SpaceX company is based in Texas. He has also spent heavily across the country as Democrats are expected to investigate Musk’s role as head of the federal cost-cutting Department of Government Efficiency if they take control of Congress.

“It’s historic,” said Taylor Bell, a 27-year-old law student, who attended an election watch party in Houston.

“Hopefully, we see money coming back to the people of Texas and not more of the same we’ve seen – well, my whole life at this point.”

US Congressman Christian Menefee, a Democrat who represents Houston, told those gathered: “Tonight, Texas has restored the hope of a nation.”

“Tonight, I believe firmly that we can accomplish anything in this country if we just stand together and we fight back against hate and bigotry,” he said.

Yvonne Nunga, a 29-year-old who works in the technology industry, said the election represented a generational shift.

“The younger generation and all the people who want a better future came out and made their voices heard,” she said. “This party, this fight right now, is not about left or right. It’s about top vs bottom, and I’m so glad that we have candidates that are making this a pivotal point in their messaging.”

“The current politics of the current administration is not working for the people,” she added. “It’s not for the people, by the people; it’s for the billionaires bought by the billionaires.”

Tuesday also saw the surprise victory of gubernatorial Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa, whose challenge had been considered a long shot even into the final days of the race.

Hinojosa will become the first Latina governor in the history of Texas despite Latinos making up 40 percent of the state’s population.

“Now I stand before you, humbled and grateful, and in awe of the incredible grace and power of God and of Texas,” Hinojosa said during a victory speech on Tuesday night.

Alejandra Peimbert, a regional communications director for Hinojosa’s campaign, said the victory should be seen as a rebuke to the hardline immigration policies enacted during 10 years under outgoing Governor Greg Abbott.

Abbott has cooperated closely with the Trump administration in its mass deportation campaign, spearheading policies that saw local law enforcement officials conduct immigration enforcement.

“I think the Latino community and our vote has been underestimated by politicians constantly,” Peimbert told Al Jazeera.

“The economy is so bad, and the horrendous things that ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] has done to our community, tearing apart families, … I think my community finally had enough,” she added.

“President Trump will no longer have a puppet in a governor.”

The state has long been a Republican bastion in the US. But Abbott’s tenure has been defined by a more hardline conservative lurch, with tough approaches not only on immigration but also to social welfare programmes, abortion rights, education and religious freedom.

Abbott’s supporters have touted rapid economic growth in recent years, spurred by tax cuts and regulation rollbacks.

Critics have argued that the economic growth measured by these metrics primarily rewards corporations and the wealthy while middle- and lower-class Texans see little benefit. Texas’s poverty rate sits above the national average, with little in the way of a social safety net.

Mandalyn Salazar, a 58-year-old Houston resident, said she was in awe following the surprise victory.

“I’m just like, right now, like, in the moment, like I just can’t believe this is happening,” she said. “We have families, and we’re all paying so much for our gas and our groceries, and I just felt like our governor – he just wasn’t getting it. I think a lot of us felt like, you know, our state, like, had been taken over by big money.”

Dylan Sutter, 21, was among the revellers on Tuesday night.

“It’s one of the biggest things Texas can ever experience, because these are two strong candidates that took their time, they took their dedication and focused with every community in Texas, and so they deserve this position,” he said of Talarico and Hinojosa.

“Everything is blue. It’s like the ballot itself was painted blue by the time we were done with it.”

articles.title: North Korea fires multiple missiles in fourth weapons launch in a month, Seoul says
articles.summary: North Korea fired multiple missiles on Wednesday toward the sea off its east coast, South Korea‘s Defense Ministry said, marking Pyongyang’s fourth such weapons launch in a month.
articles.body: SEOUL, South Korea — North Korea fired multiple missiles on Wednesday toward the sea off its east coast, South Korea’s Defense Ministry said, marking Pyongyang’s fourth such weapons launch in a month. The South Korean military detected the missiles that were fired from the Sondok area, an eastern coastal region of North Korea, the ministry said. Seoul and Washington were closely analyzing the launch and remained ready to respond to any potential provocation, it said. North Korea has carried out a series of weapons tests this year, including the launch of a missile that flew more than 550 miles as well as testing hypersonic missiles. Seoul’s announcement came hours after Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, ruled out dialogue with Washington until the U.S. abandoned what she called its hostile policy. She also repeated Pyongyang’s denial that it was behind the hacking at crypto exchange Binance after the FBI accused North Korea of carrying out the heist. The missile launch followed a North Korean media report that leader Kim Jong Un visited a naval shipyard building a destroyer and stressed the importance of a powerful naval force. North Korea’s frequent missile tests this year also suggest Pyongyang may be nearing completion of preparations for mass production, potentially including weapons for export to Russia, said Lee Choon-geun, a missile expert and board member at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology. “Before mass production and deployment, you typically need many tests,” Lee said. “Or they may be looking to export missiles in bulk to Russia, in which case they would need to run a lot of tests before shipping.”

articles.title: N Korea fires multiple missiles, denies US claims on Binance hack
articles.summary: Kim Yo Jong refuses dialogue with US after denying responsibility for theft of more than $6bn in crypto assets.
articles.body:
North Korea has fired several missiles into the Sea of Japan, according to South Korea’s military, hours after Pyongyang denied allegations that it was behind the theft ⁠of more than $6bn in crypto assets from Binance.

South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said on Wednesday that it had detected the launch of several missiles from the Sondok area on North Korea’s eastern coast towards the Sea of Japan.

It said authorities in South Korea and the United States were analysing the details of the launches.

The tests marked Pyongyang’s fourth such weapons launch in a month. They came a day after North Korea denied involvement in the Binance hack, dismissing an FBI announcement that North Korean hackers were responsible as “a trite provocation”.

Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, said on Friday that hackers stole more than $6bn in what appears to be the largest cryptocurrency heist on record.

The FBI later said North Korean hackers had orchestrated the theft, attributing it to a hacking group known as TraderTraitor, which was also behind a $1.5bn hack of the Bybit exchange last year.

Early on Wednesday, Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, said Pyongyang viewed the FBI announcement as “an extension of Washington’s invariable hostile policy toward” North Korea.

She ruled out dialogue with Washington until the US abandoned that policy.

“It is our clear stand that we have no need to sit face to face with such unreliable and hostile persons,” she said. “The choice for peace includes dialogue, of course, but this is not surely equated with national interests for us.”

US President Donald Trump said in August that he plans to meet Kim Jong Un later this year, seeking to revive the bond he claims to have forged with the North Korean leader during his first term.

Trump said it was important to “get along” with Kim, adding that Pyongyang had 57 “very powerful” nuclear weapons.

Previous rounds of talks between Kim and Trump in 2019 abruptly ended amid disagreements over Pyongyang’s nuclear programme. In October, the US, South Korea and Japan again reiterated their call for the “complete denuclearisation” of the Korean Peninsula.

The call came as North Korea has accelerated its weapons testing this year, in what analysts say is likely a bid to increase its leverage in any future diplomacy with the US.

Its recent tests have included a submarine-launched ballistic missile, hypersonic missiles, attack drones, and cluster bombs designed to be carried by ballistic missiles.

On Tuesday, Pyongyang said it had tested a new cluster warhead for strategic cruise missiles the previous day, claiming it could destroy an area of 5 to 6 hectares (12 to 15 acres) with “high-density power”.

The latest launches followed a North Korean state media report that Kim had visited a naval shipyard building a destroyer and stressed the importance of a powerful navy.

articles.title: Gillette India faces ‘pink tax’ complaint  as consumer commission issues notices to company and senior officials over allegations that women’s razors are priced 4 to 5 times higher than men’s
articles.summary: JAIPUR: The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission in Kota on Monday issued notices to Gillette India Ltd and its senior officials over a

articles.title: In 1990, Oregon trucked 580,000 tyres up to 200 miles to shore up slide-prone US 42; net cost $10 a ton, and federal engineers called it the largest tyre fill for a landslide correction project
articles.summary: In 1990, Oregon engineers tackled a landslide on US Highway 42 using 580,000 shredded tires, reducing the weight on unstable slopes and innovating waste management. This historic project was noted as the largest tire fill for landslide correction by federal authorities.
articles.body: Discarded car tyres usually create a waste management problem, but Oregon engineers found an unusual use for thousands of them during a highway repair project in 1990. A slope along a road embankment was unstable and adding more regular soil would have put more weight on ground that was already moving. Instead, the Oregon Department of Transportation (ODOT) replaced part of the heavy soil embankment with shredded scrap tyres, a lighter material that cut the load on the unstable slope. The work took place in 1990 on US 42, the Coos Bay-Roseburg Highway, about 25 miles west of Roseburg in southwestern Oregon. ODOT’s report lists the route as Oregon state route 35. The Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) later cited it as the largest known use of shredded tyres in a landslide correction project.Highway construction reactivated an existing landslideThe project was carried out in 1990 on US Highway 42, also known as ODOT Highway 35 along the Coos Bay-Roseburg route about 25 miles west of Roseburg in southwestern Oregon, which is referred to as Oregon State Road 35 in the ODOT engineering report. Modification of the embankment through Highway upgrading led to the reactivation of an old landslide underneath the road due to the increased load. The need for a repair measure that could stabilise the slope without increasing its load required a design whereby part of the soil embankment was replaced by shredded chips. The soil from excavation was used to create a counterweight at the bottom of the slope. ODOT documented the work in its February 1991 report, Experimental Project: Use of Shredded Tires for Lightweight Fill. Four suppliers delivered 580,000 shredded tyresThe job needed about 5,800 tons of shredded tyres, roughly 580,000 tyres. Four suppliers trucked them to the site from 150 to 275 miles away, according to the 1993 paper by Richard J. Upton and George Machan in Transportation Research Record 1422. The chips arrived in 100-cubic-yard trucks, each carrying 28 tons. Workers placed them in three-foot lifts and compacted each lift with a D-8 dozer. Handling the material caused some trouble. Exposed steel wire in the shreds punctured some of the dump-truck tyres used on the job. The 1993 paper by Upton and Machan covers the supply and construction in more detail.Oregon recycling program reduced the material cost to $10 perOregon’s Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) backed the project through a program that reimbursed the productive use of scrap tyres. The shredded material cost $30 per ton and DEQ refunded $20, bringing the material cost down to $10 per ton. Placing and compacting it added $8.33 per ton, for an installed cost of $18.33 per ton. The reimbursement made shredded tyres a practical option for the repair.After construction, the tyre fill got a three-foot compacted soil cap on the top and side slopes. The road surface went on top: 23 inches of aggregate base under 8 inches of asphalt pavement. The thickest part of the tyre embankment was about 12.5 feet. Under the weight of the cover, it settled about 20 inches, roughly 13 percent of its original thickness.ODOT monitored the structure with slope inclinometers, piezometers, settlement plates and survey hubs. The 1993 study found that the pavement’s initial deflection was about double the deflection over an earth embankment.FHWA identified it as the largest known landslide-correction projectThe project appeared in the FHWA’s User Guidelines for Waste and Byproduct Materials in Pavement Construction. The guidelines called Oregon’s use of about 580,000 scrap tyres the largest known use of shredded tyres in a landslide correction project. That record covers landslide repairs only, not every highway embankment that used recycled tyres. The FHWA also set up another project in Colorado where about 400,000 to 450,000 tyres were used in an interstate Highway embankment. The repair conducted in Oregon showed that old tyres could be used as a lightweight material for construction purposes, especially when normal soil puts pressure on the unstable land.You use AI every day. articles.title: St Albans teen musician is flying the flag for the recorder
articles.summary: Alma Nunez Debretzeni says "people have a stereotype that it's a beginner's instrument".
articles.body:
A 17-year-old musician who was runner-up in the BBC Young Musician 2026 competition has said she is "proud to be flying the flag for the recorder".

Alma Nunez Debretzeni, from St Albans, was one of three finalists in the competition on Sunday.

The teenager performed Graham Fitkin's Recorder Concerto in the final, which was won by 18-year-old violinist Sofia Demetriades.

"People have a stereotype that it's a beginner's instrument or a primary school one," said Debretzeni.

"People come to me and say 'I did not know the recorder can do that'."

The Year 12 student said her classmates had been "very sweet" and watched her perform on television before warmly welcoming her back to school on Monday.

She has been studying psychology, music and English at A-level at Parmiter's School near Watford, but said the contest had inspired her to follow a new path.

"I was planning on studying psychology and training to be a psychotherapist, but this whole experience has been incredibly inspiring and made me realise music is what I want to do most."

Although she also plays the cello and sings, Debretzeni said she wanted to continue showing people how versatile the recorder could be.

"The recorder has always felt natural to me, like a second voice and I feel like [it is] a way of expressing emotion."

articles.title: On patrol with the officers battling Norwich's serial shoplifters
articles.summary: Police are pledging to pursue prolific shoplifters, but how do we solve the problem longer-term?
articles.body:
Norfolk's police and crime commissioner says the force is one of the best in the country at catching shoplifters. The BBC went out on patrol with police officers tackling retail crime in Norwich.

As PC Ben Blewitt, retail beat manager for Norwich, walks through the city centre, shopkeepers come out to thank him and share the latest intelligence on serial shoplifters.

They use an app to log information and communicate with officers in real time, reporting live incidents and sharing CCTV evidence.

"Without the retailers, we would really struggle," says Blewitt.

Soon he spots a familiar face on Gentleman's Walk. It's 35-year-old John Price, who is on bail and wanted for further shoplifting offences.

Blewitt immediately arrests him – for the sixth time this year.

"You're so busy, we can't keep up with you," he tells him.

A police van arrives and takes Price to Bethel Street Police Station to be processed.

Price, of no fixed address, has already served two jail sentences this year for shoplifting and is barred by court order from entering nearly 20 stores.

For his 37 shoplifting offences this year, Price has pleaded guilty every time.

When he appears at court for his latest thefts, he is sentenced to a further six months in prison – his third jail term of 2026.

Blewitt says Price is far from the only prolific offender he deals with. In fact, he says most of his work involves the same small group.

"There's probably at any one time between 25 and 30 offenders similar to John who are going through this cycle," he says.

"We will target anyone who steals from our city. And if it's the most prolific offenders, I can assure you that we will be actively pursuing them until we get them."

Recorded shoplifting offences in Norfolk fell by 8.5% in the 12 months to the end of June .

Colin Sutton, Norfolk's Reform UK Police and Crime Commissioner, says this is an issue that police cannot arrest their way out of.

He says Norfolk Police is one of the best-performing forces in the country at catching shoplifters, but that officers are being "let down" by a criminal justice system "on its knees".

"We solve it by unjamming the criminal justice system. We solve it by sentences being more realistic," he says.

Sutton wants to see longer prison sentences for repeat shoplifting offenders.

A government spokesperson said shop theft was down 4% on last year, charges up by 19% and that it was "giving police the powers" to crack down on perpetrators.

"For too long, retail crime has been dismissed as low-level offending," the spokesperson said.

"It harms shopworkers, damages businesses and hollows out communities."

The charity Revolving Doors, which works with offenders, wants to see a complete transformation in how shoplifting is dealt with.

It says it too sees a small group of repeat offenders committing the majority of low-level crime, like shoplifting.

Its chief executive Pavan Dhaliwal says such crimes are mainly driven by "unmet health and social needs" and that sending these people to prison does not help.

"The prison sentence does nothing to address what the underlying behaviours are and what's causing them to commit those particular crimes," she says.

Often the people committing these offences are "victims of crime first", she says, and need rehabilitation services and housing rather than being locked up for a short time.

"The cost implications of the current system are extraordinarily high and they are far more costly than actually diverting people," she says.

"Taking that... prevention-first approach and ensuring people get the help that they need, it means that then you don't get the repeat offences and I think that's the real prize here."

articles.summary: Van Jones likened the Republican Party's midterm election losses to the Jonestown mass murder-suicide, calling the results a full repudiation of President Donald Trump.
articles.body: CNN analyst Van Jones celebrated the Democrats’ midterm election victories Tuesday night by comparing the defeat for Republicans to the infamous 1978 Jonestown mass murder-suicide and calling the results a repudiation of President Donald Trump. "I'm happy, happy, happy," Jones said of the election results. "I'm so happy. Listen, this is way bigger. This is like Christmas and a birthday and the Easter bunny and Halloween. This is the repudiation of Trumpism that people have been hoping for, seeing American democracy — seeing that sometimes you have kleptocratic rulers that get in power and ensconce themselves for decades in America. Twenty-four months later, ‘Knock it off, we don’t want it.'" He then compared the GOP losses to the mass murder-suicide at the Peoples Temple commune in Jonestown, Guyana, where more than 900 people died after cult leader Jim Jones directed his followers to drink cyanide-laced beverages. "And by the way, if you join a cult at some point, the cult leader takes you to Jonestown and tries to get you to drink the Kool-aid. This is Jonestown for the Republican Party," he said. "They drank the Kool-aid, and they have candidates that are dropping like flies across the country because they did not stand up to this guy when he was doing things that were wrong, when he was violating the law, when he was running over our system, they didn‘t stand up to him, and they‘re paying the price." articles.title: Halloween: Parents' warning after they say metal objects 'found in sweets'
articles.summary: Parents from Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland say they found metal objects in Halloween sweets.
articles.body:
Two mothers have spoken of their shock after discovering metal pins hidden inside sweets collected by their young children while trick-or-treating.

"If he had of swallowed that, he would be sitting in hospital right now and it would've been a completely different story," Samantha Bingham said, after finding a metal needle inside a chocolate bar collected by her eight-year-old son.

Savannah McDaid said she was shocked to discover four "metal pins embedded" in sweets collected by her three-year-old son after they returned home from trick-or-treating together.

The incidents are being investigated by police, with parents being warned to inspect any remaining sweets collected over Halloween.

Samantha told BBC News NI that the discovery had left her deeply shaken.

"We check his Halloween sweets every year, we had never had any issues in previous years but we always check," she said.

"We had heard about using a magnet before so I checked them over and I was actually surprised when one of the sweets was caught by the magnet and I was gobsmacked when I found the needle inside."

Samantha said her son Kaiden was also left extremely frightened by what had happened after trick-or-treating in the County Down village of Rathfriland.

"Kaiden just went pure white. There were tears and everything and [he] actually threw out all of his other sweets because he was so scared afterwards."

She said she could not understand why anyone would want to put a child at risk in such a way.

"My heart actually sunk," the mother-of-two added.

Samantha has appealed to other parents to carefully check any remaining children's Halloween sweets, urging them to be vigilant and look out for anything unusual.

"Who or what is the reason for it?" she asked.

"It's just shocking that someone could potentially do something like that to an innocent child."

Savannah McDaid and her three-year-old son Arló had enjoyed an evening trick-or-treating together, in their home town of Stranorlar, County Donegal, in the Republic of Ireland.

It was only when they returned home that Savannah's mother suggested checking Arló's sweets.

Savannah said her mother had previously seen videos online of people finding objects in Halloween sweets, although she admitted she had not given the possibility much thought before.

"We checked over the sweets with a fridge magnet and four of the sweets actually reacted to them and stuck to it," she told BBC News NI.

They decided to examine them after they responded to the magnet's pull.

"It was two chewy bars and two chocolate bars and then when I opened them there were little clothes pins, like metal pins embedded inside them."

She said she was shocked by what she found and worried about what could have happened if her son had eaten the sweets.

"He would never have thought twice about checking the sweets, because he is only three. He is just so innocent that way.

Savannah said she had also heard about another mother in neighbouring Ballybofey who had discovered "metal pin-like objects" in her son's sweets as well.

"It's just scary that something like that could happen and I reported it to the Gardaí (Irish police), but we are not sure if they could ever find who done this, because it would just be so hard to trace."

She said the incident had left her feeling hyper-vigilant about any future sweets he receives but was incredibly thankful she had checked the sweets before her son had a chance to eat them.

The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) has confirmed it is investigating a report received on Tuesday of a "chocolate bar contaminated with a needle" in Rathfriland.

In a statement, a PSNI spokesperson said: "Inspect all wrapped and unwrapped sweets collected during 'Trick or Treating' and look for any unusual tears, pinholes or broken seals.

"Anyone finding anything suspicious or signs of package tampering should avoid handling the item further and contact police immediately."

In a statement, An Garda Síochána (the Irish police service) said they received a report of an incident which occurred on 31 October in the Stranorlar area and Ballybofey area in relation to children's trick-or-treat sweets.

articles.title: Republican Susan Collins loses seat, ending almost 30 years in the Senate
articles.summary: Maine's Senate race was mired in controversy after Democratic nominee Graham Planter withdrew following multiple scandals.
articles.body:
Democrat Troy Jackson has defeated longtime Republican incumbent Susan Collins in Maine, unseating the famous moderate senator in a race marked by controversy.

Jackson entered the race after replacing Graham Platner, the Democratic nominee who withdrew following a series of scandals.

First elected in 1996, Collins was the only Republican senator representing a state that has consistently voted Democratic in presidential elections since 1992.

She has cultivated a reputation as a moderate and sought to distance herself from President Donald Trump during her campaign. Jackson, a former logger, campaigned on workers' rights and accused Collins of yielding to pressure from the president.

Collins and Jackson went head to head during state debates, with Jackson making national headlines when he told the 73-year-old to "shut up".

He entered the campaign late in the season, after Planter withdrew following a series of controversies, including allegations of sexual assault. Platner has denied the allegations.

Jackson had failed to win the Democratic gubernatorial primary, but won the senate nomination in a special convention. He positioned himself as a working-class candidate and backed progressive policies like abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

His victory over Collins allows Democrats an even larger majority in the US Senate, after wins in several key states - including Texas and South Carolina - gave them control of the chamber.

Democrats also won control of the US House of Representatives, meaning they will control all of the US Congress for the last two years of Donald Trump's presidency.

Collins at times walked a tight rope with Trump. A moderate Republican, in a state that historically supported Democrats, she often criticised his policies.

She was viewed by many as a possible "swing vote" during controversial legislation, who could tip the scales either way.

She voted to convict Trump in his second impeachment trial in 2021, after the riots at the US Capitol, and also voted against Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill, which passed.

And she voted against repealing the Affordable Care Act, helping to save the health-care policy commonly referred to as Obamacare.

Yet she backed the president in many crucial votes - including voting in favour of Brett Kavanaugh's nomination for the Supreme Court and confirming Robert Kennedy Jr, a vaccine sceptic, as Health Secretary.

In debates, Jackson tied Collins to Trump's record, pointing to her voting record and arguing that she could have used her position as a key swing vote to sway the president.

Collins, though, argued she used her position leading the Senate's Appropriations Committee, which oversees writing bills that allocates federal funds to states and programmes across the US, to make a difference for Maine and its residents.

articles.body: Conservatives were left stunned by the results of the 2026 midterm elections Tuesday and are attempting to grapple with the new political landscape. Democrats dominated in red and blue states alike, easily retaking both the House and Senate, as well as flipping several governorships. Democrats picked up victories in numerous states won by President Donald Trump in 2024, including seemingly deep-red spots like Texas, South Carolina, and Kansas. Members of conservative media were gobsmacked by the sweeping defeats. "It is a catastrophic night for Republicans," Washington Examiner columnist Guy Benson reacted on FOX. DEMOCRAT SEIZE HOUSE CONTROL IN STUNNING BLUE TSUNAMI, VOW RETRIBUTION AGAINST TRUMP ADMIN "Sometimes you get your a-- kicked, and deserve it. Tonight is one such time for the Republican Party," conservative radio host Buck Sexton reacted to the results on X. "Way too many mistakes. Bad messaging. Poor candidates. High prices. Unnecessary war that did not go as promised. We get up tomorrow and carry on. But there are lessons here." "Tbh most Republican candidates this cycle were uninspiring, lazy, and thoroughly ineffective communicators. I’m not all that surprised by some of these outcomes," Trump advisor Alex Bruesewitz said. HUGH HEWITT: THE GHOSTS OF 2006 ARE STIRRING — BUT WILL THEY CATCH THE GOP? "[Trump] picked a bunch of the bad ones," commentator Mary Katharine Ham wrote on X of the losing candidates. Many pointed to Trump, the war with Iran and the surge in gas prices as being responsible for the devastating losses for his party. "Trump launched an unpopular and pointless war. Gas prices are too high. People can’t afford groceries. Trump abandoned the American First message. This is why Republicans are getting crushed. It’s very simple," The Daily Wire's Matt Walsh wrote. "This will be the biggest national wipeout for Republicans since 2006, when voters brutally punished the GOP for an ill-advised and poorly planned war in the Middle East," The Federalist co-founder Sean Davis said. However, conservative radio host Erick Erickson insisted the issues went far beyond the Iran war and gas prices. "It was also the corruption. The incompetence. The tariffs. The playing nice with Russia. The impression of cruelty. The overly aggressive deportations. The accidental arrests of American citizens who were Hispanic. The arrogance. The ballroom. The reflecting poll. The golf courses. The arch. The Qatari 747. The aggressive redistricting push. The threats against enemies," Erickson listed. The "Ruthless" podcast hosts appeared on Fox News Channel and joked about leaning towards hard liquor as the night progressed. "I don't think this was, at all, concerned with policy. This is a firm backlash," Josh Holmes told Fox News' Bret Baier. "This is an absolute backlash from the voters," Comfortably Smug agreed. They aren't concerned with any kind of vision for the future that the Democrats are offering or how they're going to fight inflation… They are angry, and they're making their voices heard." articles.title: Sterts Theatre Arts and Environmental Centre receives lifeline
articles.summary: Charity considered going into administration before loan allowing it to continue for a few months.
articles.body:
The Sterts charity, which is responsible for the theatre and studio buildings on Bodmin Moor, in Cornwall, has been given a stay of execution after a member offered a loan of £20,000.

In September the Sterts Community Interest Company, its operational arm, went into voluntary liquidation leaving a number of creditors unpaid.

The Sterts Charity is still functioning but before the loan offer was made it asked members at its AGM if it too should go into administration owing to its current deficit of £12,000.

Member Vickie Bishop, who offered the loan, said: "I've kept the doors open and what it means is that for the next five months they [theatre groups] can use the facilities there."

The Sterts Community Interest Company has refused to comment since it went into voluntary liquidation, however, the separate organisation the Sterts Charity held its AGM last week.

Trustees told members three investors were in negotiation about taking on the theatre acting as a limited company but the trustees would not disclose the names at this stage because of confidentiality reasons.

Members were also told the 2025 accounts showed a deficit of £130,000 and that there had been a big drop in income by 62% and an even bigger drop in donations by £92%.

Bishop said when the new administration took over operations two years ago "we were categorically told that am-dram wasn't part of their plans".

She said: "And I had particularly had an interest in bringing the youth theatre back.

"It never happened they talked about it and they talked about having various groups I wonder how much of it was just to tick boxes for funders."

Bishop said "there was a will" to keep the theatre and studio open.

"The community want it, you only had to look at the people that were at the AGM and the enthusiasm and the number of people that were volunteering to do things.

"Nobody wants it to fail, even if they're cross about what happened in the past, nobody wants Sterts to close forever; nobody wants to bring the curtain down so to speak; we all want it to succeed."

Nick Buckland, chair of the Sterts Charity, said: "At the moment we are balance sheet solvent because we have a big asset in the site.

"We're running very close to the limit in terms of our operational funding and that's really what we're concerned about as trustees.

"But with the offers of help we've had we should be able to continue to work in a good way for the next few months."

Buckland recognised that Sterts needed to have more community engagement which he said "was partly lost in the past".

Asked about why the CIC went into voluntary liquidation he said it was really a case of the number of tickets being sold and there were bids for funding "that didn't come off, it was a combination of factors".

"We can get it back to an even-keel if we get the right support now, " he said.

He said he believed Sterts could be saved.

"Oh, I hope it can, I wouldn't be here if I didn't think that.

"I've been involved in quite a number of things were we have turned it around and I hate losing," he said.
